The bank locked me out at 7:40 on a Monday morning, which is a bold time to start anything. Three wrong guesses. I was so sure the first one was Biscuit, because Biscuit was the dog during the years I opened that account. Then I remembered it might have been during the Murphy years. Murphy had a number too. I think it was his birthday, but I never knew his birthday because we got him from a man in a Walmart parking lot. The reset email went to an address I stopped using in 2017. I am now on hold. The music is lovely.
column6: My husband keeps all of his passwords in a little notebook in the desk drawer labeled PASSWORDS in big block letters. I told him that's the first place a burglar would look. He said a burglar is welcome to his Netflix. I've started borrowing the notebook myself.

column2: My friend Deb came out of the fitting room on Saturday in a lime green dress with ruffles at the shoulders and asked me to be completely honest. She said completely. She said it twice. So I told her it made her look like a very confident salad. I said it kindly. I even smiled. She stood there for a good ten seconds with the face of a woman whose car I had just walked past with a key. Then she bought the dress. She wore it to lunch the next day and sent me a photo. It still looked like a salad.
column6: I have been asked for my honest opinion maybe four hundred times in my life and it has gone well exactly twice. Both times it was about a casserole. I'm starting to think people want a mirror that talks, not a friend. I'm not available for that position.

column2: My daughter asked me last week what I did after school when I was eleven. I told her the truth. I got off the bus at 3:15, let myself in with the key on a shoelace around my neck, ate a sleeve of saltines standing up, and left. Where did you go, she asked. Out. With who. Whoever was outside. When did you come home. When the news came on, or when I got hungry, whichever came first. She looked at me like I had survived a shipwreck. I didn't have the heart to tell her it was the best part of the day.
column6: My mother's entire tracking system was opening the back door and yelling my name once. If I didn't answer, she assumed I was fine and went back to her show. I was always fine. I have no idea how, but I was always fine.

column2: My friend Carol set me up on a coffee date last Saturday because she said I needed to put myself out there. He was on time, which I'll give him. Then in the first nine minutes he told me about his ex-wife, his other ex-wife, the woman he almost married in 2009, and a lawsuit involving a boat. He asked nothing about me. Not one thing. When he went up for a refill I sat there doing math on how many more ex-wives might be coming. I finished my coffee, thanked him kindly, and drove straight home to my couch. Carol has been informed.
column6: Carol called Sunday morning to ask how it went. I told her about the boat. There was a long silence on the line and then she said, well, at least he was on time. That's the bar now, apparently. I'm keeping my Saturdays.

column2: My grandmother had a fur coat and a cocktail ring. I have a heated blanket and a coupon for 20 percent off. We are not the same.
column6: Grandma Ruth wore that cocktail ring to the Piggly Wiggly every Tuesday like she was attending a gala. I wore my heated blanket to the mailbox this morning. It has a cord. I had to unplug it first. She would have had a lot to say about that.

column2: Last night I did everything right. Teeth brushed, lamp off at 10:20, the good pillow flipped to the cold side, blanket tucked under both feet exactly the way I like it. The cat settled on my legs. My whole body let out the long sigh it saves for the end of the day. Then, about forty seconds into true happiness, my bladder cleared its throat. I lay there and negotiated. I told it we could wait until morning. It said we could not. So the blanket came off, the cat was offended, and the whole ritual started over from scratch.
column6: I've started making a final lap to the bathroom before bed whether I need it or not. My husband calls it the pre-flight check. Last night I did the pre-flight check and still had to get up at 2:10. Some flights just get delayed.

column2: Tuesday afternoon outside the farmers market, the handle on my canvas bag gave up and eleven apples went rolling down the sidewalk in eleven directions. A man in a fleece vest stopped and asked if I was okay in the voice you use on someone standing on a ledge. A woman behind him asked if I needed to sit down. I did not need to sit down. I needed my apples. Meanwhile, the big maple across the street was dropping leaves by the thousand and people were stopping to take pictures of it. Nobody asked the maple if it was okay. Nobody ever does.
column6: I collected nine of the eleven apples. The other two rolled under a parked truck and I decided they belong to the truck now. I told my husband about it that night and he asked if I was okay. I made him sleep with the window open.

column2: Monday I couldn't remember the word for spatula and called it the flat flipper in front of my sister-in-law. Tuesday the man at the deli counter said have a nice day and I very nearly climbed over the glass. Wednesday a dog food commercial came on, a golden retriever waiting at a window for a little boy, and I cried so hard I had to pause it. Thursday I woke up at 3:40 a.m. fully awake and roughly the temperature of a toaster. I have stopped trying to predict anything. I just get up and see who shows up.
column6: I keep a small fan on the kitchen counter now, one in the car, and one in my purse. My husband calls it my fleet. Last week I turned all three on at once in the grocery store parking lot. Nobody said a word. Smart people.

column2: I bought a $6 candle called 'Serenity' and I've been waiting all week for it to kick in.
column6: The candle has been burning on the kitchen windowsill since Monday night. So far this week the dryer has broken, the dog ate a sock, and I've been on hold with the cable company twice. It smells wonderful, though. I've lowered my expectations to smelling wonderful.

column2: There are four rooms on the first floor of this house and by 7 on a weeknight all four of them have someone in them. The TV is going in one. Someone is on speakerphone in the kitchen. The dog has claimed the couch and is not negotiating. So I've started taking my glass and a book upstairs to the little window at the end of the hall, the one nobody uses because it doesn't have an outlet. No outlet means no chargers, which means no visitors. I sat up there for an hour on Tuesday. Nobody noticed I was gone. Perfect.
column6: My husband found me up there last night and asked what I was doing. I said reading. He asked what I was reading. I held up the book. He stood there a little longer, so I turned the page very slowly and he finally went back downstairs. It's a good book.

column2: At the neighborhood potluck on Sunday, a grown man in a golf shirt picked up a decorative pinecone off the table and asked if it was the dessert. He was serious. His wife had to take it out of his hand. Ten minutes later a woman two houses down explained to me that she doesn't wear sunscreen because she has a base tan from 1994. Then someone microwaved a foil pan. I stood by the punch bowl and quietly made my peace with every warning label I've ever laughed at. They know exactly who they're writing for. I've met him. He took a pinecone.
column6: I went home that night and read the back of my dishwasher pod tub just to see what else it says. It says keep out of reach of children, and there's a little picture of a man who looks a lot like the pinecone guy. I'm not saying it's him.

column2: On Thursday I walked into the garage, stood there for a full minute, and walked back out with nothing. I still don't know what I went in for. That same afternoon I ran into a woman I've known for twelve years at the pharmacy and called her Linda. Her name is Brenda. Then the dentist's office called to ask where I was, and the answer was the pharmacy, calling Brenda Linda. On the drive home the radio played one song from 1988 and I sang every single word, both verses, the bridge, the ad-libs. My memory works fine. It just has priorities.
column6: My husband tested this at dinner. He asked me the name of our accountant and I got nothing. He started humming a song from junior year and I finished the entire second verse with hand motions. He just nodded and wrote the accountant's name on a sticky note for me. He's learning.
